utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Today we will continue with the submissions in this matter. Before we continue, however, may I say that although the matter has been set down for hearing tomorrow, the Chamber intends to conclude hearing submissions today, and we ask for the cooperation of the parties. Each party has been assigned 45 minutes. There is no obligation to utilise all that time, and many of the arguments have already been made, and instead of repeating them, you can simply say that you adopt them. Nonetheless, there is no intention on the part of the Chamber to restrict any speaker. Is there a problem? So we will hear from Mr. Johnson for the United States.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOHNSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Before I begin, I just wanted to briefly pick up a point yesterday that was raised about the status of NATO. My understanding is that NATO has prepared a letter that they have either sent to the Court or that will be on its way today, so I just want to alert Your Honours to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Johnson.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOHNSON
utterances.text: The United States appreciates the opportunity to be heard by Your Honours on this important matter. The position of my government is detailed in the written submissions we provided on February 28, 2003. In keeping with Your Honours' decision yesterday, I will endeavour to keep this presentation in open session. The argument I will advance this afternoon is straightforward. First, the Defence requests its frame to directly, unreasonably and unnecessarily implicate issues of extraordinary national security sensitivity. The Defence yesterday characterised the request as an extraordinary one, and on at least that matter we agree. We're asking you to consider the national security aspect of it, not as a basis for rejecting the request outright, but because it underscores the need to hold the Defence to the high standards in meeting the requirements of Rule 54 bis. Also, the Tribunal's Rules and jurisprudence provide an established and workable framework for protecting a state's national security while facilitating the provision of information to either the Prosecution or the Defence. Second, as outlined by my colleagues yesterday, the Defence has not met the requirements of Rule 54 bis, by failing to take reasonable steps to obtain the requested information cooperatively, failing to adequately identify the information to which the application relates --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Kindly slow down for the interpreters, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Did you hear that, Mr. Johnson? The interpreters are asking you to slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOHNSON
utterances.text: You've heard the request could be reframed so as to both minimise the national security concerns and better meet the requirements of the Rule. Finally, the United States has offered to share the information with the Defence on this basis, and the Defence has refused. Because the Defence has failed to meet the prerequisites for an order under Rule 54 bis, we submit that the application must be rejected. As a threshold matter, we believe it is useful to review the framework that the Tribunal has established to make it possible for governments to provide relevant information in a way that safeguards national security equity. This framework underscores the obligation of a requester to work cooperatively with the requested state. And it also explains why requests that impinge on national security should be held to the high standards in meeting the requirements of the Rule. There is no dispute among the parties that the Defence request involves matters of core national security sensitivity. The Defence concedes in its application that its request "creates a difficult tension" involving national security interests. Defence counsel's e-mail to the United States on August 14, 2002, which is contained in the annex to our submission, admitted, "Frankly, I expect that this request is going to create some tension between the right of the government to protect its intelligence information and the right of the accused to discover relevant material." This is immediately evident by looking at the wording of the request. The first and second parts explicitly reference intercepts, or signals intelligence. The third part in referencing "sources of information working on your behalf," seeks access to human intelligence reporting. None of the three parts of the request specifies beyond a reference to the accused's name the content of the information sought. Rather, it is --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Kindly slow down for the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The request has been repeated for you to slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOHNSON
utterances.text: -- of the information itself. Framing a request in this way not only contravenes the specificity, relevance, and other requirements of Rule 54 bis but also unnecessarily exacerbates the acute national security concerns. There is no doubt that information requests centred on intelligence sources and methods go to the heart of state security and sovereignty. I'd like to elaborate a bit on this point in light of Judge Bonomy's question yesterday. The state's ability to protect such sources and methods, including not to reveal their existence, scope, and use is fundamental to their effectiveness. When such information is released, it compromises not just the information itself but the source or method that was used to gather it. With respect to intercepting communications, the issue is not, as Judge Bonomy pointed out yesterday, whether this type of capability exists generally; rather, it is whether it has been applied in particular circumstances, how it is applied, its effectiveness, the degree to which it is used and the scope of that capability. With respect to human intelligence, it relates to the protection of sources whose lives could be endangered by the release of the information they provide. Such a compromise of these intelligence methods in turn can jeopardise the ability of a state to collect information and protect itself against terrorists and other adversaries. The Tribunal, in its Rules and jurisprudence, has consistently strived to address the difficulty tension referred to by Defence counsel by providing for information sharing in a framework that protects national security equities and rigorously scrutinises requests that threaten them. As this Chamber is aware, Rule 70 prohibits the Prosecution from disclosing information provided on a confidential basis. Under this Rule, the Trial Chamber may not compel a witness to answer any question relating to the origin of the information if the witness declines to answer on the grounds of confidentiality. The Appeals Chamber, in ruling on the interpretation and application of Rule 70 in the Milosevic case, explained the necessity of these protections. The Rule, it said, was "Designed to encourage states and others to assist the Prosecution or the Defence." It encourages cooperation by "guaranteeing information providers that the confidentiality of the information they offer and of the information sources will be protected. Without such guarantees of confidentiality, it is almost impossible to envisage this Tribunal being able to fulfil its functions." So how do the rigorous protections of confidential information and the sources of that information afforded to states under Rule 70 context relate to Rule 54 bis? Or put differently, how is it that the Tribunal will go to extraordinary lengths to protect sensitive information in the Rule 70 context, even to the degree of curtailing judicial inquiry into the information itself but that same information can be put at risk when subject to a request under Rule 54 bis. We would submit that the answer lies in the Blaskic case. There, the Appeals Chamber distinguished between cooperative and compulsory approaches in dealing with states. It adopted the view that "cooperative process should wherever possible be used, ... it should be used first, and ... resort to mandatory compliance powers ... should be reserved for cases in which they are really necessary." Now, under this paradigm, the state must be given every reasonable opportunity to avail itself to the protections afforded under the cooperative process governed by Rule 70 before it is confronted with a compulsory process under Rule 54 bis. Otherwise, Rule 70 would be largely an empty letter, since either the Prosecution or the Defence can skip over the cooperative process and go directly to a compulsory one. It seems to us that it would be incongruous for a situation to be created where states are entitled to clear protections safeguarding their national security interests when they share information cooperatively with the Prosecution or the Defence under Rule 70. But for them to be deprived of such guaranteed protection because they were precluded by the requester from entering into a cooperative framework. It is for these reasons that Rule 54 bis and the Blaskic decision requires a requester to take reasonable steps to obtain information cooperatively from a state. As my colleagues have detailed, the Defence has made at best a token effort at working with states. In the case of the United States, our protracted efforts at trying to work with Defence counsel cooperatively are detailed in the annexes to our written submission. A brief review illustrates both our commitment to trying to work cooperatively and the Defence's predisposition to move to a compulsory process. The United States responded to the Defence's original request by proposing to hold a meeting to discuss it and the modalities that we have used successfully in responding to past Defence requests. On August 14, 2002, the Defence rejected this offer, foreshadowing that the real desire was to seek a compulsory order. The Defence said, "It would be better for you to put any questions or concerns about our request in writing rather than arranging a meeting." This is "So that the ICTY Trial Chamber can have an accurate record of our efforts to obtain voluntary compliance prior to seeking a binding order." This is before our dialogue has even begun. A week later, the United States urged counsel to reconsider, explaining that such discussions in our experience were "A constructive first step in formulating a mutually agreeable approach towards providing requested information to Defence counsel in the manner that protects important US government equities relating to sensitive information." On August 22, the Defence agreed to the proposed meeting and provided the assurance that, "We want to do whatever it takes to cooperate with you in getting access to information relevant to General Ojdanic's case." On September 19th, the United States met with counsel. We detailed the approach used in successfully entering into information-sharing relationships with other Defence counsel. We reiterated our willingness to cooperate similarly. We emphasised that while we would not confirm or deny the existence of the requested intercepts, we would search all, all sources for information responsive to a proper request and do our utmost to provide responsive information in some form. On September 28, 2002, the Defence submitted a revised and more narrowly focused information request. The revised request excluded statements of a personal or social nature, focused on statements relating to Kosovo, and it focused on statements made by the accused rather than anybody else in Yugoslavia. Although improved, the revised request remained deficient in a number of respects, including by continuing to focus on the means by which the information sought was collected and memorialised rather than its consent, rather than the substance of the information itself. While this search was ongoing, however, Defence, contrary to its earlier assurance about doing "Whatever it takes" to cooperate abandon that process. On November 13th, Defence filed the present application and reverted to its original, unfocused, and intrusive request language. In filing such an application only six weeks after presenting its revised request and in the midst of US government efforts to respond to it, the Defence demonstrated that its interactions with the United States were less for the purpose of arriving at a cooperative framework to obtain the requested information than for documenting their superficial efforts to satisfy this requirement of the Rules. Despite the application, the United States continued to process the request. On January 24, 2003, the United States informed the Defence that we had identified potentially responsive information. We noted that none of the material located contained exculpatory information and that no such information was being withheld, and we said we would provide it to the Defence as soon as it took steps to safeguard our security interests by obtaining an order from the Tribunal applying Rule 70 and executing an agreement to protect the information while it was in their custody. We explained that these protections sought were equivalent to those that we have requested from the Prosecution whenever we have shared similar information, and that the protections were the same as those we had obtained from all other Defence counsel who have desired access to sensitive US government information. How, then, did the Defence answer this offer of information responsive to their request? On January 29, the Defence rejected it. Despite the rejection, the United States made one final effort to provide the Defence the information it had requested. On February 3, 2003, we sent a letter "To make clear that the US government's offer of responsive documents is not conditioned on the Defence withdrawing its motion as it relates to the United States government." In other words, that there was no downside, no cost to the Defence pending this information. More than a year and a half has passed since the United States made this offer, and we have received no reply from the Defence. It's difficult to reconcile this indifference with the Defence's assurance the previous August to do "Whatever it takes with the United States to obtain this information," but more importantly it's impossible to reconcile such an approach with an obligation under the Tribunal's Rules and precedent that the compulsory process should be one of last resort and used only in cases where it is really necessary. The request also fails to meet the other prerequisites established by the rule and the Blaskic decision as discussed by my colleagues yesterday. These relate to the requirements to identify the documents, establish their relevance, demonstrate necessity, and ensure that the request is not unduly onerous. Because the purpose of these elements is to prevent unwarranted intrusions into a state's sovereignty, it follows that a request that intrudes into the matters that are at the heart of a state's security interest such as intelligence that those requests should be strictly held to meeting these -- the high standards of these requirements. With respect to specificity, Rule 54 bis requires that the party requesting an order "Identifies as far as possible the documents or information to which the application relates." The Blaskic decision explained that the request must "Identify specific documents and not broad categories." The application concedes that the request is for a "Category of documents" rather than specific ones, but it relies, or tries to rely, on a selective quotation from the Kordic case to suggest the documents could be requested by category where it is impossible to specify the title, the date, and the author of each document, and where the requested category of documents was identified as "Sufficient clarity to enable ready identification of the documents falling within that category." Now, while the Appeals Chamber in Kordic did impose those requirements, it imposed an additional one that Defence counsel did not mention, and that is that "The requirement of specificity clearly prohibits the use of broad categories," and the emphasis is in the original Kordic decision. Also, the categories at issue in the Kordic case were based on the content of the information sought, not on the type or form of information. It's difficult to envision broader categories of request than ones which encompass all of the accused's utterances written and oral during a six-month period and all of the utterances by anybody else in Yugoslavia relating to Kosovo in which the accused was mentioned or referred to. As my colleagues mentioned, the requests were so broad that they sweep up everything from social chatter to family conversations to business dealings. The three parts of the original request, including in many ways the revised request, fail to specify the participants beyond the accused in these conversations, the location where the statements were made, the approximate dates where they were made, and more importantly, their content. These kinds of requests represent the classic fishing expedition where the requester is not searching for a particular piece of evidence he has reason to believe exists but is casting a very broad net in the hopes that something useful might turn up. This approach is prohibited by the requirements of Rule 54 bis, and it was rejected by Judge Hunt in the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. quoted excerpt that was read by my Canadian colleague yesterday. The fact that the Defence is unwilling or unable to describe the content of the information it seeks cannot provide a basis for it to evade the requirement of specificity. Rule 54 bis in the applicable case law also require that the requester indicate how the information sought is relevant to any matter at issue before the Judge or Trial Chamber. The submission asserts in a conclusory manner that evidence of statements made by or to General Ojdanic are relevant to show whether he participated in the offences, whether war crimes were reported to him, and his mental state concerning the events. Now, the problem with this justification is that it presumes a request that focuses on statements by either the accused or others relating to the elements of the crimes charged. In fact, the request has no such limitation and extends to almost any statements by the accused or others with respect to the accused within the six-month period. The Defence desires intercepted communications for the period irrespective of what those purported intercepts actually say. The Defence tries to justify the relevance of statements that have no links to the crime at issue by asserting that they demonstrate that the accused "Despite being intercepted on X number of calls was never heard to order, instigate, plan, aid, or abet -- plan, aid, and abet, condone, or fail to prevent or punish a war crime." In other words, more than two dozen states are being asked to produce broad categories of sensitive intelligence so the Defence can attempt to demonstrate by the purported absence of information relating to the crimes that the crimes were not committed. Now, even accepting for the sake of argument that a request of this sweep was permissible, the justification, the logic behind it is fundamentally flawed. The absence of inculpatory information in the material sought would openly be significant if one assumed that every one of the accused's communications during the relevant period had been contained, retained, located, and reviewed, which is an impossibility. Even then, one wouldn't know whether the absence of inculpatory information reflected a lack of criminal intent or an intent to avoid inculpatory communications. To satisfy the relevance requirement, the information sought must be linked to the charges at issue, and a request that fails to differentiate between such statements and those unrelated to the crimes charged has manifestly failed to meet this requirement. Rule 54 bis also requires that a requester show that the information sought is necessary to a fair determination of the matter at issue. This distinguishes the approach of the Tribunal under Rule 54 bis, which is a tightly controlled regime from the much broader discovery regimes that are applicable in various national systems and particularly the American one with which both Defence counsel and I familiar. The Defence's submissions do not address this requirement beyond stating it. First, by encompassing huge quantities of material that are not relevant to the matters at issue, the request is clearly not necessary to the adjudication of the accused's guilt or innocence. Second, even with respect to statements of the accused or others that might be relevant to the trial, states are neither the only nor the best source of the requested information. The accused is in the best position to know what he said, when he said it, and with whom he spoke or wrote to about relevant matters. The accused is also in the best position to know who the participants were in these exchanges so they can be corroborated and so that testimony, if applicable, can be sought. The accused obviously will not remember every single communication made during this period, but presumably ones that are relevant to the matters at issue in this trial would be the kind that would be recalled if they were, in fact, made. Moreover, if the information sought was actually necessary to the matters at issue in this case, why did the Defence rebuff two offers from the United States to provide responsive material? Why has the Defence left unanswered for more than 18 months an offer to provide the responsive material without prejudice to its pursuit of the current motion? Beyond these Rule 54 bis requirements, the Tribunal's jurisprudence identifies two other factors for a Chamber to weigh before it will proceed with a compulsory order against states. I'll touch on them briefly. First, the request must not be unduly onerous. In making this assessment, the Blaskic court made clear it a Chamber would not -- would consider not just whether the identification and location of the information is "overly taxing," in the words of the court but also the burden imposed by the "scrutiny of the documents for release. The scrutiny of the documents for release." The request must also be "strictly justified by the exigencies of the trial." Now, it is obvious that a request involving either the breadth of the one at issue in this application encompassing every communication of an individual during a six-month period and every mention of him by other individuals and all communications originating in the former Yugoslavia and related to Kosovo, or the fact that the request involves intelligence of the highest sensitivity, that processing it would be onerous. Without going into the details of intelligence sources and methods, it is reasonable to assume that highly sensitive information, whether it is acquired through technical or human means is closely compartmented and segregated. The fact that the request itself seeks "Summaries, notes or text," of the purported statements, necessitates a search through hard copy files rather than just electronic ones. Even beyond the intelligence material sought, the request for "All correspondence, memoranda reports, recordings, or summaries" of statements made by the accused to US officials or sources would again necessitate a hard copy search that could cover dozens of different offices in dozens of different agencies and departments as well as our embassies abroad. Moreover, the sensitivity of the sources and methods at issue means that even if responsive information is located, it must undergo an individual, painstaking, and multi-layered review process - this is the scrutiny referred to in Blaskic - before that piece of information can be authorised for release. So even assuming that some responsive information was stored electronically, that it has been retained on a database, that the database is located, and that the responsive information is filtered from the other information produced by the word search suggested by Defence counsel, that search represents only a fraction of the burden involved in actually producing responsive information to this request. As a final matter, the United States has consistently been among the strongest supporters of the Tribunal and few states, we believe, have provided cooperatively as much information, in terms of both quality and quantity, to both the Prosecution and to the Defence. The Blaskic Appeals Chamber noted both the relevance of a state's good faith in assessing a request for a compulsory order and also observed, quoting the Prosecutor, that "The mandatory compliance powers expressly conferred by Article 29 of the Statute will rarely, if ever, need to be invoked with respect to ... third, in other words, not former belligerent states." Here it is worth noting how different the situation here is from other cases where the Office of the Prosecutor has made repeated, increasingly specific requests from countries whose former officials are being tried by the Tribunal and where those requests have been repeatedly rejected. None of the states that are the subject of this request have an equity in the outcome of these particular proceedings, apart from seeing that justice is done fairly and impartially, and all of us have expressed a willingness in cooperating with appropriately framed requests from either the Prosecution or the Defence under the Rules of the Tribunal. With respect to the specific request before the Chamber, the United States believes that the record of our dealings with the Defence counsel demonstrates that we have at every step not only responded in good faith but gone the extra mile to make relevant information available in response to the request. In conclusion, the United States submits that the Defence request has failed to meet the key prerequisites outlined in Rule 54 bis as well as the Blaskic decision and the other Tribunal jurisprudence. The request is over-broad. It encompasses a vast quantity of irrelevant material. Information sought is not necessary for a fair adjudication of the issues. More fundamentally, it implicates directly and unnecessarily information of the highest national security sensitivity. The national security nature of the information enforces the obligation of the requester to work with states to obtain the information cooperatively before proceeding to a compulsory process. And it also requires that the request be held to the high standards in meeting the prerequisites of the Rule. The Defence, however, has failed to meet its obligation to take reasonable steps to obtain our cooperation. Any steps it took were only after the repeated urging of the United States, and even those were abandoned. Despite these failures, the United States has acted in good faith and located responsive information, and we offered to provide the located information under conditions equal to those required of the Prosecution that would protect our national security equities while permitting a sharing of it. The Defence rejected our first offer and has responded to our second one with 18 months of silence. Under these circumstances, the accused's application for a compulsory order to produce information, we respectfully submit, must be denied. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Johnson, I have two questions for you. The first is this: What do you mean when you say that the application focuses on the means of recovery rather than the product?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOHNSON
utterances.text: What I mean to say is that the request is phrased in terms of focusing on intercepted communications. That is the focus of the request. It's augured around intercepted communications rather than being focused on the actual content that is sought in these communications. So it keys off of the intelligence method used to gather the information rather than keying off of the content of the information that is being sought.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But that's simply a factor of the lack of specification in the application, really, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOHNSON
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It could delete these words and the application would just be the same. You could delete from each of paragraphs 1 and 2, or A and B, the words "of any intercepted communications."

utterances.speaker: MR. JOHNSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All you would need to put in was communications -- or just delete the word "intercepted" and you would have the same application without the point you make. So the real focus should be on the lack of specification, should it not?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOHNSON
utterances.text: I think it is certainly on the lack of specificity. I guess the way I look at it, Your Honour, is that the request is in two parts and there are separate problems with respect to each part. On the back end of the request there is the lack of specificity about what the content sought actually is. On the front end there is a problem that it focuses specifically on -- on an intelligence method used to gather the information whereas that concern could be alleviated by either deleting that language or a more general formulation such as "all information of" and then specifying the content of the information sought.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Now, the second -- just give me a moment to note your response. The second question is about the mechanics of a hypothetical situation. I would like guidance on how this Tribunal, or indeed the state involved, would tackle a situation where an order was made by the Trial Chamber requiring production of material, and once the state in question identified or completed the exercise of identifying the material, it found that some of it was of such sensitivity that it did not want to produce it or was anxious about producing it, that's probably a better way of phrasing it. How, within the Rules of the Tribunal, do you envisage that situation being tackled? And I'm raising it now because it arises here as a result of the broad nature of the application and the potentially broad nature of any order made which doesn't focus on individual items of material and it doesn't really give you a chance at the moment to say just what you might be concerned about in relation to any particular item.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOHNSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I agree. I think the way -- well, I'd like to answer that in a couple of respects. First, in the experience of the United States, we have never faced that situation, because in every case, with the hundreds of requests that we have received from the Prosecution and the Defence, we have always found a way that we can provide the requested information in a form that is responsive to the request but also secures our national security, and that is why we place such emphasis and I placed such emphasis in my oral submission on this being a two-phased process that requires the cooperation first, and only when that doesn't work, to get to the second phase because our experience is that that can resolve these issues. If you get to that -- and that it is much easier in that first phase where you have a Rule like Rule 70 that can provide its own framework for protection, that that gives states the most flexibility in working with the requester to avoid these very difficult issues. And I'm reluctant to address hypothetically what would happen beyond that but I would --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are you actually saying that Rule 70(F) could be applied at the stage at which you have found material? It would be difficult, because that Rule's confined to the accused or the Defence counsel making the application. So it doesn't give scope for a state, when ordered to produce material, to come here and say, "Well, we'll produce it but under certain conditions."

utterances.speaker: MR. JOHNSON
utterances.text: No, I agree, Your Honour. I think that kind of exchange happens before you proceed to the compulsory process.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I follow that, and I understand your argument entirely on this. What I'm trying to work out is, assuming we're not dealing with that situation - and I stress it's a hypothetical question - how do you envisage the United States tackling the question of the -- having their anxiety, their concerns addressed before the material is released or indeed not released?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOHNSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think once you get to that second stage it becomes -- it becomes very difficult, and there the answer would depend very much on the -- each individual specific piece of information that was at issue. Some of them main not present great sensitivities or ways may be found to deal with those specific pieces. Other pieces may present the highest sensitivity and may require their own -- their own handling. I know, as Your Honours are aware, the Blaskic decision goes into this a bit as does the second part of Rule 54 bis once you get to that stage and the types of protection that can be applied then, including, in extraordinary cases, limiting the actual review of the information itself. So those modalities are provided to some degree by the Blaskic decision and by the back end of Rule 54 bis, but again the ability to apply those would depend very much on being able to know what it is that you are talking about, what piece of information is at issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOHNSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Johnson. Thank you. The next submission will come from Professor Tomuschat on behalf of Germany, or am I mistaken.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOMUSCHAT
utterances.text: Your Honour, the agent for Germany would like to speak first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, he may speak.

utterances.speaker: MR. LÄUFER
utterances.text: Mr. President, distinguished members of the Tribunal, it is an honour to appear and act before this Court as an agent of the Federal Republic of Germany. Allow me first to me express my highest esteem for members of this Tribunal. I would like to accentuate that Germany has always supported the Tribunal to the best of its abilities. This political and legal commitment to the common rule of law will persist. Your Honours, Germany's grateful for the opportunity present today its comments on the admissibility and well-foundedness of the application of the 15th of November, 2002, which is still pending before this Tribunal. After my short introduction to my position, Professor Tomuschat, as counsel for the federal republic of Germany, will present our arguments, whereafter I will again ask for the floor to present the submissions of Germany. Germany commented on the application by counsel for General Ojdanic on its submission of the 27th of February, 2003, arguing in particular that the search for and identification of the materials requested would be disproportionally burdensome. By our submission of the 20th of June, 2003, counsel for the applicant sought to remedy the flaws of their request by explaining in some detail why in their view the Trial Chamber should grant the order they had applied for. This attempt has failed. Even in light of the explanations provided, the application does not meet the criteria specified in Rule 54 bis of the Tribunal's Rules of Procedure and Evidence, henceforth called Rules. Neither have counsel for the applicant sufficiently identified the documents or information to which the motion relates, nor have they indicated how these documents or information are relevant to the pending proceeding or demonstrated that Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. these materials are necessary for a fair determination of the matter. At the very outset, Germany would like to emphasise the importance it attaches to a loyal cooperation for all Member States of the United Nations with that Tribunal. It may be recalled that the very first person who stood trial in The Hague, Dusko Tadic, was surrendered by German authorities to the Tribunal. There is no need to stress that the Tribunal can live up to its responsibilities only if the states to which it addresses its orders bona fide comply with such orders. In the instant case, too, Germany is prepared to cooperate with the Tribunal within the limits specified by Rule 54 bis as interpreted in the case law of its Appeals Chamber, but it is clear that these limits have to be respected. Germany has already deployed its best efforts with a view to facilitating the task of the Tribunal in the case of the applicant, General Ojdanic. As mentioned in the submission of the 27th of February, 2003, a comprehensive and diligent search conducted according to a criterion of reasonableness in the main archives produced no materials covered by the categories described in the application of the 15th of November, 2002. At the very outset of this pleading, it can be said that no new information of any relevance would be discovered if the Tribunal granted the application as requested by the Defence. In that sense, the dispute over the application has already become moot. However, the request raises issues of principle. Germany, therefore, gradually avails itself of the opportunity provided by this hearing to articulate its reservations and objections with regard to request for the production of documents which are as broadly framed as the application of the 15th of November, 2002. Mr. President, I would now kindly ask the Tribunal to give the floor to Professor Tomuschat as counsel for Germany.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Professor Tomuschat.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOMUSCHAT
utterances.text: Mr. President, distinguished members of the Court. It emerges from a simple perusal of the motion of 15 November 2002 that the Defence has failed to identify the material sought or does so only in a formal way, by requesting just anything where the name Ojdanic will appear. This failure, which was not remedied by Counsel's intervention yesterday, is not in conformity with Rule 54 bis. The -- this provision seeks to confine the obligation encumbered upon states by enjoining a requester to specify in detail what it wishes to obtain. Requester states on the basis of Article 29 of the Statute and Rule 54 bis of the Rules must be limited in scope and weight. After the decision of the Appeals Chamber in Blaskic of 29 October 1997, Rule 54 bis was included in the Rules, which now provides specifically that a moment under Rule 54 shall, and I quote "Identify as far as possible the documents or information to which it relates." This clause is obviously meant to implement the holding of the Appeals Chamber in the Blaskic decision that any request for the production of documents must identify specific documents and not broad categories. The phrase "As far as possible" cannot be stretched to mean no identification at all in instances where an applicant does not even know what should be identified. A narrow interpretation of Rule 54 bis is not only suggested by its wording but also by its general purpose. Third states which are not directly involved in a trial can play only a subsidiary role in proceedings before the Tribunal. It is a task incumbent upon the Prosecutor to carry out the requisite investigations and to prepare an indictment if appropriate. On the other hand, the Defence will be ensured by counsel it has never been the intention of the Security Council in adopting the Statute of the Tribunal to shift the burden of Prosecution or Defence on the individual members of the international community. Third states can and should lend their assistance to the Tribunal so that justice may be done. But according to the philosophy of the Statute, their function remains a complementary one. They cannot be burdened with the full weight of tasks which either the Prosecution or the Defence shall have to fulfil. Additionally, it should be noted that in the Blaskic case, the Appeals Chamber rightly saw some merit in the distinction between states located on the territory of the former Yugoslavia and third states not directly involved in the conflict and whose role was confined to that of concerned bystanders. To be sure and -- it was -- this was discussed yesterday also, this distinction was characterised by the Appeals Chamber as having some value only for practical purposes, but it again reflects a criterion of proximity or remoteness, as the case may be. Primarily, it is incumbent upon the parties proceeding before the Tribunal to see to it that justice be administered correctly. Germany was in no way involved in the actions which constitute the factual basis from which the indictment against the applicant arose. Its obligations stem from its being a member of the United Nations and, therefore, being placed under the authority of the Security Council. However, even the powers of the Security Council are not boundless, which the Security Council itself recognised by setting forth in Article 29 of the Statute a duty of cooperation which is tantamount to saying that the Tribunal and the states members of the United Nations shall work together in a mutual relationship of trust and confidence on a level of equality. The limitation ratione materiae of orders enjoining a state to produce relevant documentation is clearly indicated in Article 29 of the Statute. It emerges from a careful reading of paragraph 2 of that provision that states are required and can be ordered to perform specific acts with a view to providing assistance to the Tribunal. But all the examples given in paragraph 2 concern such specific acts, starting with the identification and location of a person and ending with the surrender or the transfer of an accused to the Tribunal. Nowhere does the Statute demand that states engage in general activities of a comprehensive character designed to clarify whether a person may have committed criminal acts or whether he or she has led a fully law abiding life. States can be requested to add bits and pieces, which may, of course, be extremely important, to proceeding which is directed and steered by others. But they cannot be pushed into an investigatory role. Identifying and collecting evidence essentially remains in the hands of the parties proper acting before the Tribunal. According to a general understanding of international criminal law, judicial assistance means assistance with regard to acts specifically identified. It does not appear that this traditional pattern of judicial assistance, as it has been shaped in bilateral or regional frameworks and as also reflected in Article 93 of the Rome Statute was totally set aside by the Security Council in adopting Resolution 827. To be sure, this Tribunal has a special status. Its powers go beyond the obligations which states have generally entered into by virtue of international agreements. Yet the Member States of the United Nations are not placed in a relationship of hierarchical subordination vis-a-vis the Tribunal, as borne out by the use of the term "cooperation." Enjoining states to furnish the Tribunal with the full content of their archives would change that relationship in a dramatic fashion and impose upon them burdens which could only be justified with regard to an aggressor state or a state otherwise threatening international peace and security. The distinction between a state targeted under Chapter VII of the Charter and a third state providing assistance to the Security Council of the Tribunal must be maintained and should not be blurred in proceedings before this Tribunal, which was established under the authority of the Security Council. Now some words about the relevance of the materials sought. It has already been stressed in many of the submissions made to the Tribunal that the request as formulated by counsel for the applicant also fails to meet the criterion of relevance listed in Rule 54 bis and specified more in detail in the Blaskic decision. This objection applies to all of the three heads of the request. It is openly acknowledged in the submission of 20 June 2003 and was confirmed yesterday by Counsel Robinson that the Defence does not know of any relevant piece of information in the possession of the states concerned that might contain exculpatory elements in favour of the applicant. Rather, the Defence hopes that, amid masses of materials it wishes to get hold on, there might be some indicia showing that the charges brought against the applicant are unfounded. And be referred to paragraphs 7 to 20 of submission of 20 June 2003. In this sense, the request can indeed be equated with an attempt to introduce the contested concept of discovery, which has its legal home in the United States, into the current proceeding. Counsel have commenced a fishing expedition which they believe might disclose some elements of proof that are beneficial to their client. They are admittedly unable to show or even to contend that the materials they wish to be presented to the Tribunal may contain elements susceptible of exonerating the applicant. The net which they have cast does not just see to catch fresh fish from a little pond, it rather attempts to sweep an ocean with anything the waters contain, like those drift nets which the General Assembly has condemned so many times. Such comprehensive search for such facts and information is not authorised by Article 29 of the Statute. States as third parties are not subject to the jurisdiction of the Tribunal to the same extent as private parties in litigation taking place before ordinary courts, according to one specific domestic legal order. I'd again like to refer in this connection to the persuasive opinion of Judge Hunt on the motion by Esad Landzo to preserve and provide evidence which was already quoted yesterday by counsel for Canada, and I refrain from again quoting that sentence. The over-broad scope of the request becomes abundantly clear if one reflects just for a short moment on the effects of the actual implementation of the different subitems of the request. All of them encompass material that have no relation whatsoever to the pending proceeding. According to subitem (A), all recordings, summaries, notes, or text of any intercepted communications to which General Ojdanic was a party would have to be produced. This definition would not only include materials deriving from official military activities of the applicant but also from his private conversations with his family, his friends, with his tax authorities, his planning of a vacation trip or his religious authorities. It stands to reason not only that such communications have nothing to do with the charges brought against the applicant but that it would also be highly problematic to divulge the contents of conversations or other communications, and the secrecy of which third persons may have a vested interest. Furthermore, it does not serve the interests of justice to inundate the Tribunal with masses of irrelevant documentation. In the case of other defendants, tonnes of materials might have to be shipped to The Hague if the Tribunal granted the motion and the precedent thus set then determined the further procedural course of this Tribunal. Easily thus, applications under Rule 54 bis could be used to hamper or outright obstruct effective administration of justice. In any event, this reflection makes once again clear that the aim of the defence is not to compel the states concerned to open their archives with respect to specific documents, in accordance with the gist of Rule 54 bis, but to get access to possible sources of evidence that might be of some interest to the applicant. Subitem (B) is even more objectionable. Essentially, the Defence wishes to get hold of anything recorded in any form whatsoever where the name of General Ojdanic is just mentioned. Here the relevance of the material sought is obviously lacking in its totality. It is the Tribunal which is called upon to try the applicant, General Ojdanic, and not the marketplace of public opinion. What third persons expressed about the applicant, how they evaluated him and his way to conduct the war is clearly irrelevant to the outcome of the proceedings. At Nuremberg - and I jump back into the past - nobody was interested in learning more about the appraisal in the capitals of the world of the major Nazi war criminals during World War II. The accused were made accountable for their deeds in accordance with general standards of fair trial. Their conduct was gauged against the legal yardstick laid down as a statute of the military tribunal, and of course, international customary law. For that purpose it was not necessary to know what had been said about the accused, perhaps even with some sympathy, before the outbreak of the war, later in a generally condemnatory way. It stands to reason that the intelligence services the Allied powers during the Second World War had to do their utmost in order get a clear picture of the leadership of the Third Reich and of their thinking. And they assumed that information was collected on a daily basis. A request similar to the one made in the instant case, extending over six or even 12 years, would have taken years to be implemented and would have been totally irrelevant. What matters are the facts, the criminal acts, and not their mirror image in expert or public opinion. Although it is in principle up to the Tribunal to assess the relevance of the materials sought, and this is the decision of the Appeals Chamber of Kordic of 9 December 1999, there must be certain limits to what can be requested. Here it is apparent on the face of the application that it is entirely unable to unearth anything of importance for the adjudication of the pending charges. In such instances of manifest lack of relevance, the Tribunal must reject the request. Regarding subitem (C) it is again utterly unclear what relevance all oral or written statements made by the applicant can have for the outcome of the proceeding. It may well be that some of these materials could exonerate the applicant or, on the other hand, prove his guilt. The request is not confined to such relevant materials. It extends to just any information and therefore necessarily for the most part the materials without any importance. Now some words about the necessity of the materials for a fair trial. Additionally, any observer would find it extremely difficult to understand why the applicant needs the assistance of third states in order to know what he said and declared during the period concerned. He himself must have archives, at least a diary from which he should be able to glean what contacts he had during the relevant time. Contrary to what was said yesterday by counsel for the applicant, the relevant six months cannot be just a Black Hole in the memory of the applicant and his written notes covering that period. Consequently the simple consideration makes it abundantly clear that provision of the materials identified in subitem (C) of the application is not necessary for the purposes of a fair trial. The submission of 20 June 2003 seems to have been written on the basis of the assumption that the defendant has to prove his innocence. This assumption grossly misunderstands the premises of a trial based on the rule of law. We wish to emphasise again what was said yesterday by counsel for Canada and the United Kingdom. It is the Prosecutor who must present the evidence which shows that the indictment is well-founded. If she fails to prove her case, the indictment will have to be rejected. The applicant will be acquitted. Apparently the Defence intends to obtain negative evidence to the fact that the applicant did not commit any of the offences he is being charged with. Such an attempt to prove a negative cannot be successful. Even if in hundreds of conversations no reference was made to any war crimes or other crimes, such finding would not exclude that on another occasion criminal acts were ordered or approved. This has just been explained in detail by counsel for the United States. Germany considers, furthermore, that the research as requested by counsel for the applicant is much too burdensome even for a well-organised administration. Materials that will have to be scrutinised are scattered over a vast array of federal and in some instances also Laender authorities, the component units of the Federal State of Germany. Some of the materials are stocked in electronic form, others are not that easily accessible. Thus for the most part, the archives would have to be reviewed individually by trained specialists. Such search through hard copy files entails huge costs and is again a consequence of the over-broad framing of the request. Lastly we refer to national security interests. Germany must furthermore reserve its right to invoke its national security vis-a-vis a possible order by the Tribunal that would grant in full the request by counsel for the applicant. No state can be obligated to reveal details about its system of collecting intelligence regarding all currencies beyond its borders. The interests of national security are explicitly recognised in Rule 54 bis (F) of the Rules. Here again, the inadmissibly broad scope of the request makes itself felt. Even in the eventuality that the Tribunal should grant the request by counsel for the applicant it may not be possible to immediately raise objections regarding the content of the materials concerned. In fact, at the time of delivery of such an order it would not at all be clear what documents might be encompassed by it. German authorities would have to commence a huge search operation and only after determination of such operation would it become known whether the disclosure of any specific elements resulting from the search would negatively affect German security interests. However, provision of the available resource materials would in any event give decisive clues as to the organisation of the system Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. according to which Germany collects information as to occurrences outside its borders. Accepting the demands of the Defence would be tantamount to revealing to the public at large, in particularly also to foreign governments, the way Germany runs its intelligence services. This inevitable consequence is again related to the over-broad scope of the application as underlined by Judge Bonomy a couple of minutes ago. If specific information on a specific issue had been requested, the relevant data could be provided without such far-reaching, harmful consequences; however, pieces of information spread out over six months coming from different sources could easily be used by others to put together the pieces of the puzzle with a view to obtaining a comprehensive picture of the system. Mr. President, I have come to the end of my presentation and may I request you to kindly give the floor to the agent for Germany, Mr. Läufer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, he has the floor. Mr. Läufer.

utterances.speaker: MR. LÄUFER
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, I will now present the conclusions and submissions of Germany. It is plain that the applicant -- that the application of the 15th of November, 2002 has been drafted in such broad terms that it conspicuously exceeds the scope of Article 29 of the Statute and Rule 54 bis of the Rules. In its present form the motion cannot be granted. The Defence of the applicant would have to substantially modify the requests filed through the application of the 15th of November, 2002 in order to bring them within the purview of the relevant provisions of the Statute and the Rules. Germany, therefore, respectfully prays the Tribunal to reject the request. I thank the Tribunal for its kind attention in listening to our oral arguments. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Läufer. Professor Tomuschat, may I ask you a question? I was interested in the -- in the general comments that you made at the beginning of your submissions about Article 29, which derogates from customary international law protecting the sovereignty of states. Are you saying that to the extent that there is this derogation it should be interpreted conservatively in the interests of the protection of state sovereignty?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOMUSCHAT
utterances.text: Mr. President, Germany favours a broad interpretation of Rule -- of Article 29 of the Statute, but on the other hand, we emphasise the fact that Article 29 of the Statute speaks of cooperation and this in paragraph 1. And I think the word "cooperation" is a decisive concept there, and it underlines that there must be mutual trust and confidence and that a proceeding must be conducted on a cooperative basis. I think this is what I wanted to -- to underline. We think that cooperation must be the key concept in construing Article 29 of the Statute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And that is why the applicant must first exhaust all steps -- I'm saying and that is why the applicant is required to take all reasonable steps to secure the information before moving to the compulsory regime.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOMUSCHAT
utterances.text: Mr. President, Germany did not mention the steps which were taken in 2002 by the Defence. Germany received a letter, indeed, but this letter was also couched in very broad language, in the same way as the application and, therefore, the relationship or the -- this -- well, motion on the part of the Defence did not go very far, because it was felt on the part of German governmental authorities that this was simply too broadly framed, that they could not respond in a positive way to the request made first by the Defence for the applicant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor Tomuschat. We will now take a break of 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We'll now hear submissions on behalf of France from Ms. Dubrocard.

utterances.speaker: MS. DUBROCARD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, first of all I would like to say that it is a great honour for me to appear for the first time before you on behalf of the French government. I'm given the difficult task to speak -- to speak last following the presentations of all the participants at the present hearing. I am not going to test your patience, and I'm going to try to focus on the main points of my presentation, and I'll try to avoid, as much as possible, to repeat the arguments already laid out by the other state representatives. I should not be speaking more than 15 minutes. First of all, by way of an introduction regarding the proceedings before today's hearing, I would like to point out the two following points as was mentioned by Mr. Robinson several times when he made his submissions yesterday: The Trial Chamber initially decided in its scheduling order dated 26 November, 2002 that the applicant had, and I quote "fulfilled the requirements of Rule 54 bis (A) insofar as he had identified, as far as possible, the document or information to which the application relates." And where the requested document relates to the charges brought against him, and I quote again, "insofar as they relate to his acts and behaviour and insofar as he has taken steps to obtain the assistance of the concerned states and organisations." And that is why the Chamber decided and ordered the request to be served on NATO and the states mentioned in the request. However, following the comments, written comments submitted by the states, including France, your Chamber issued a new order on the 13th of May, 2003. I don't think Mr. Robinson mentioned the order yesterday. What is said in the order? You're asking the applicant to "submit a further submission addressing in more detail the relevance of the materials sought to the matter in issue in this case and specifying to what issue each recording, et cetera, is relevant." On the 20th of June, 2003, the applicant filed further submissions following the order just mentioned, and on the 2nd of September, 2004, following a stay in the proceedings, the Chamber decided to hold today's hearing. After having recalled these facts, I will now move on to the matter at the heart of the present hearing. According to the French government, the question here is whether, following the filing of the further submissions of Mr. Ojdanic on the 20th of June, 2003, it can be considered that Mr. Ojdanic has fulfilled the requirement of Rule 54 bis (A). According to us, the answer to that question is no, because notwithstanding the filing of these further submissions, the requirements set out in the Rule have not been met. This will be the object of the first part of my presentation, because the French government submits that the provisions of Rule 54 bis (A) have not been complied with in this case. I will not come back to the Blaskic judgement that led to the drafting of Rule 54 bis. I will just note that following this Rule and this case law, any party requesting an order for the production of documents or information has to, in the request, first of all identify, as far as possible, the documents or information to which the application relates; secondly, indicate how they are relevant to any matter in issue before the Judge or Trial Chamber and necessary for a fair determination of that matter; and thirdly, explain the steps that have been undertaken by the applicant to secure the state's assistance. Furthermore, such a request should be relatively unonerous. What is the situation in this case? Well, we have to say that the requests submitted by Mr. Ojdanic, even when we look at the further submissions of 20th of June, 2003, does not fulfil these requirements. With regard to the steps taken by the applicant, the French government should like to remind that in its letter dated 29th of June, 2002 to Mr. Ojdanic's counsel following their first request for assistance, the government said that in principle it was ready to cooperate with the Defence, but also noted that the request was not specific enough. Therefore, the applicant's counsel were invited to redraft their request and narrowing the scope of the request. However, Mr. Ojdanic's counsel believed that France was not a position to cooperate with them on the ground that our national law to adapt the Statute of a Tribunal to our national jurisdictions does not make it compulsory for French authorities to cooperate with the Defence. The reference to in the legal framework from our letter from 29 June 2002 should not be interpreted as a refusal to cooperate, because in the same letter, we expressly stated that we were quite ready to examine any request of assistance related to the disclosure of specific information or documents. Following this misinterpretation of our response, the Trial Chamber deemed that the requirement related to steps to be taken by an applicant to obtain the assistance of a state had been fulfilled, but we should repeat once again here that France has never refused to provide assistant to Mr. Ojdanic's counsel but only has requested specificities about the nature of the request submitted. Secondly, with regard to the identification of the documents and to their relevance, the lack of specificity of the request has not escaped the attention of the Chamber, because in your order of 13th of May, 2003, you expressly demanded from Mr. Ojdanic that he indicate the relevance of the materials sought to the matters in issue in the case, and also you asked him to specify to what issue each recording, et cetera, was relevant. In other words, the applicant was invited to show, pursuant to the provisions of Rule 54 bis (A), he was invited to show the relevance of the documents and the specificity with regard to the matters in issue. First of all with regard to the specificity requirement regarding the documents requested. When reading the further submissions of the applicant, we have to come to the conclusion that he does not give any specificities about the three categories of documents he has identified and that he requests. I would like to remind you that we are talking about recordings of telephone conversations in which he was a direct party between the 1st of January and the 20th of June, 1999; secondly, conversations related to him and originating from the Republic of Yugoslavia; and thirdly, any document related to his statements during the same period. By identifying these three categories of documents, Mr. Ojdanic is trying to identify the ground for which each one of these categories is relevant to the crimes he's charged with. But in reality, the difference of distinction between these three categories of documents seems artificial, because in every case, the idea is through conversations he's had or statements he's made, the idea is to reject all charges that were brought against him. We are actually talking about one single category of material, a very broad category of material drawn up between the 1st of January, 1999, and the 20th of June, 1999, and the only common element between all these documents is the mention of the name of the applicant and the fact that all these documents would be susceptible to exonerate him. Quite obviously such a wide request, such an unspecific request does not fulfil the requirements of Rule 54 bis (A). If the Blaskic judgement is the yardstick decision when it comes to defining admissibility of production of documents, other decisions were taken later and confirmed the criterion that had been set up. Yesterday, Mr. Robinson mentioned the decisions taken by the Trial Chamber in the Milosevic case where the Serbia and Montenegro had to produce, pursuant to Rule 54 bis of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, a number of documents, but he omitted to say that at the same time, the Chamber rejected many of the motions or requests submitted by the Prosecution on the ground that such requests were too broad in their nature and that they were unduly onerous. I'm referring here to an order issued by the Chamber on the 12th of June, 2003, referring to a motion submitted by the Prosecutor on the 13th of December, 2002, where he, among others, requested access to military documentation drawn up or compiled by a specific military unit between August 1991 and January 1992, and, of court, or, and I quote, "Documentation from the assembly of the Republic of Serbia between 1991 and 1992." In the Simic, Tadic, Todorovic, and Zaric case, it is true that the Trial Chamber, presided by yourself, I believe, Your Honour, granted the request of Todorovic for the production of documents held by SVO [as interpreted]. Such request -- that request was related to a very specific event, i.e., the circumstances of the arrest of Mr. Todorovic. But in this particular case, the request for Mr. Ojdanic does not deal with any specific event and is similar to what many here have called a fishing expedition. This fishing expedition is based on a number of assumptions that are set out at paragraph 16 of the further submissions filed by Mr. Ojdanic's counsel on 20th of June, 2003, and these assumptions are the following: First of all, it is assumed that a great number of conversations by the accused were intercepted; secondly, this was done without him being aware of it; thirdly, this will make it possible to prove that it -- he was not aware of the crimes that were brought against him. In English: [In English] "Evidence of the acts and state of mind of the accused than his contemporaneous statements during the times of the events when he's not aware that his conversations are being recorded or reported." [Interpretation] In reality, counsel of General Ojdanic have no idea of the contents of the documents requested, but they hope that after reading them, supposing that such documents exist, they will be able to discover some elements which might exonerate their client. In any case, contrarily to what has requested from your Chamber to the applicant in the Chambers decision of 13 May 2003 the applicant made no effort to specify to which issue in particular related each of the recordings of documents requested. He confined himself Zec to enumerate the three broad categories of documents for which he requested production and describing in general the charges against him. Coming, then, to the relevance of these documents in relation to the questions or the issues in the present case. The French government is of course aware of the case law, in particular, in the Kordic judgement, which was yesterday quoted by Defence. While it is obvious that the evaluation of the relevance or not of such documents solicited is finally to be determined by the Chamber, it remains that the states which are requested may have their point of view known. In this case, according to us, the relevance of these documents for which Mr. Ojdanic requests production is particularly difficult to assess precisely because of the too broad nature of the information requested. Even in the further pleading, Mr. Ojdanic has not established a sufficient link between the documents which he wishes to see disclosed and the facts for which he is charged. According to counsel of the applicant, their request is irrelevant because it concerns whatever be the category of the documents in question, the fact of establishing the facts which -- with which the accused is charged. But if such an explanation as broad as it is were to be accepted, the criterion requirement of relevance would become moot because it is always possible for an accused to request production of documents by giving us a reason for his request, the search for establishing his innocence. Finally I get to the last requirement which is the admissibility of an application requesting production of documents, which is to say the request concerning the -- the criterion concerning the execution. From the Blaskic case, you can see that any order of production of documents should be relatively easy. As the Judges have said in the Kordic case, I cite: "A party cannot request hundreds of documents, particularly when it is evident that the identification, location, and scrutiny of such documents by the relevant national authorities would be overly taxing and not strictly justified by the exigencies of the trial." In this case, the lack of precision of the request ruminated by Mr. Odjanic which I have spoken about would inevitably have the effect of making excessively onerous any research of the document which have been requested. Those are very varied. Not only recordings of telephone conversation which would have been intercepted but also letters, correspondence, notes, reports, the summaries of any declaration made by the accused during a period of six months. The identification is also quite vague since only the name of General Ojdanic would be the common factor. Further, it is always open to discussion whether it is necessary to produce these documents. Indeed, it would be surprising to see that only NATO and the states which are the object of such an order would be in a position to furnish such documents proving the innocence of the accused without him having also such information at his disposal. General Ojdanic was in a better position to know which reports, notes, and correspondence he wrote and received during the relevant period, which statements he may have made during that period, and which were the meetings to which he attended or still which conversations he may have had with his collaborators. It is difficult to think that he has himself kept no trace of these -- of such exchanges. For all the reasons which I have mentioned, France therefore considers that the application presented by Mr. Ojdanic does not satisfy the conditions given in Rule 54 bis of the requirements, Rule 54 bis (A) of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence and requests respectfully your Chamber to dismissal. In the alternative and only in the alternative, I wish to speak Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. very briefly on the question of the possible prejudice to interest -- to national interests by the present application. If not withstanding what has been shown your Chamber were nevertheless to consider that the application of the accused is at least partially justified, in part justified, and therefore by consequence and joint with the state's concern to produce the documents, France intends to reserve as need be the possibility to raise objections by reason that the divulgation of certain documents requested would prejudice its own interests of national security. Nevertheless such an objection cannot be envisaged in the present state of the formulation of the application because its character is -- its nature is so I am precise that it does not enable the French government to determine what are exactly the documents which have been requested by the Defence. Mr. Presiding Judge, Your Honours, I wish to thank you for your attention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Dubrocard. Mr. Robinson in reply.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, members of the Trial Chamber. I want to thank my learned friends for their excellent advocacy. They have made many objections, but we cannot lose sight of the fact that a man's life is at stake here, and that man is the accused General Ojdanic. The countries sitting here in this room are in possession of evidence that can make a difference between freedom or imprisonment for the rest of his life. Those are the stakes here as you do the difficult job of balancing the interests of the accuse at the Tribunal and the interests of the state that have the information. It's not an academic exercise. Let's fast forward to 2006. Instead of sitting over there, let's imagine General Ojdanic is sitting in the witness box and he testifies that he never ordered any war crimes to be committed, that he was unaware of any plan to expel Albanians from Kosovo, and that his standing orders from which he never varied were that war crimes were to be prevented and punished. He testifies that he had many conversations with other leaders in the former Yugoslavia and that he was never told of any plan to expel Albanians from Kosovo. He testifies that he had many conversations on a daily basis with members of his staff and subordinates about what was going on in Kosovo, and none of the murders, rapes, and destruction of cultural sites described in the indictment were ever brought to his attention. He says that when he spoke over the telephone, he gave instructions consistently that war crimes were to be punished and prevented and even ordered that paramilitaries involved in such activities were to be shot on sight. Imagine as you're hearing this testimony, would it be relevant to hear intercepted conversations involving General Ojdanic during this time period if they were available? Would it be necessary to a fair determination of those issues? The obvious cross-examination would be: What evidence do you have to back up these claims? You saw this in the Milosevic case with General Ivasov last week. Even members of the Trial Chamber were asking for corroborative information. That's what we're trying to do by this request. Let's look at how the intercepts we do have from Croatia would enhance your fact-finding process. It would be easy to imagine Mr. Nice or another Prosecutor suggesting to General Ojdanic that on the 8th of February the KLA took eight soldier of the Serb army hostage and on the 15th of January, Serb forces murdered innocent villagers in Racak and to ask him, "Isn't this just another exam of Serb forces responding with disproportionate use of force and committing war crimes to retaliate?" General Ojdanic could testify that there was no link between these two events and you may or may not believe him, but because we have the intercepted conversation from Croatia on the 8th of January, a conversation between President Milosevic and General Ojdanic, we know that their discussion regarding the capture of these eight soldiers and what to do about it was to negotiate. There was no discussion of committing war crimes or of any retaliation. Does that help you as a finder of fact? Of course it does. Is it relevant? Is it necessary? I submit that as careful finders of fact, that's the very kind of information that you want. Now, let's look at the use to which intercepted conversations have been put to at this Tribunal. In the Srebrenica cases, the Trial Chambers have been able to follow the event minute by minute in realtime thanks to hundreds of intercepted conversations provided by the Bosnian government. In the case of General Krstic, the Appeals Chamber reduced his sentence by 15 years when it was determined through an intercepted conversation that the Bratunac Brigade, which were under his command, were not the ones who executed prisoners at a place called Branjevo farm. In the Brdjanin case, in a decision on 3 October 2003 on the Defence objection to intercept evidence, contemporaneous intercepted conversations were deemed to be so relevant that they should be admitted into evidence even if the interception was illegal. So sitting there listening to General Ojdanic's testimony in 2006, you'd have a huge responsibility. You have to get it right. And I would think you would want to have every tool possible at your disposal to help you in that task. Now, think back to this hearing. You could say, "I had the opportunity to get these intercepted conversations back on the 2nd of December of 2004. Why didn't I get them?" Well, the states have fought vigorously not to give them. They said the requests weren't specific enough, the intercepts were relevant. They weren't necessary. The applicant didn't go the extra mile and that national security interests prevented them from even confirming that such intercepts existed. Let's look at these objections and see if they really justify keeping this crucial evidence from the trier of fact. Specificity. What is the function of the specificity requirement? I think it's useful to look at this in terms of two piles. Somewhere in the archives of an agency in a capital in one of these states, an analyst is sitting with that state's universe of General Ojdanic's intercepted conversations. Let's say those papers are stacked one metre high. This analyst would have your binding order and would read its terms, and he's going to go through those intercepts and put them into two piles, one pile to be delivered to the Trial Chamber, the other to stay buried in the archives. The specificity of your order will determine which pile the document goes into. Let's take social calls, something referred to first by the Government of Canada.
