I will tell you that during the war, General Ojdanic had no social life and it's very likely to be many social calls. But let's say that, for example, on the 23rd of March 1999 General Ojdanic invited a friend to his flat for a plumb brandy. If your binding order excludes social calls, that intercept will go into the pile that stays in the archives in Ottawa, and maybe that's fine. On the other hand, maybe there will be evidence during the trial from a Prosecution witness who says that General Ojdanic was in Kosovo on that day instructing the troops. Then the social call becomes important to the trial. So which pile should the social call go into? Is it better to have it in the hands of the Trial Chamber or in the archives in Ottawa? That's your call. But when deciding the fate of someone's life, do you want to gamble and leave it buried in the archives? That's why our request doesn't exclude social calls. Let's take the suggestion of the government of Netherlands that the binding order be limited to those conversations bearing on General Ojdanic's participation or mens rea for the crimes. If that suggestion is adopted, an analyst in a basement somewhere in The Hague will be reading that intercept and making the determination about whether the conversation bears on General Ojdanic's participation or state of mind. If in his opinion with his limited knowledge of the case, it does not, then the conversation will stay buried in the archives. Is that what you want? Or is it better that the intercept go into the pile for the Trial Chamber so that you can determine with your knowledge of the case whether it has a bearing on any issue of the case. What do you think is the more responsible way to discharge your duties as the finder of fact? Professor Greenwood has suggested that the request might be limited to specific, major meetings in which General Ojdanic participated in. First of all, during the war, General Ojdanic had meetings every day. All of his meetings and telephone conversations dealt with the war. He was on the job 24/7. But let's say we were required to limit our request to the major meetings. Now, somewhere in the archives in London the analyst is there separating the metre of conversations into two piles. He comes across a conversation between General Ojdanic and a subordinate in which General Ojdanic is told that the army was not involved in Racak and therefore they have no need or duty to investigate or punish anyone for what happened there. Since this conversation did not take place in a major meeting, it gets put in the pile that stays in the archives in London. You never see it. You never know it exists. And you're called upon to make a finding of whether General Ojdanic has command responsibility for failing to punish the perpetrators of the killings at Racak. The United States suggests that the conversations be limited to those relating to the elements of the crimes charged. And there is the same problem. An analyst in Washington is deciding conversation by conversation whether it relates to any of the complex elements of the complex charges here at this Tribunal. Is that how you want to make your decision with critical evidence sitting in some archive? And what happens when ten or 20 years from now some other analyst decides that the Kosovo war is ancient history and declassifies all these intercepts? They become public. Then it turns out your finding of fact were wrong. What kind of legacy would that be for this Tribunal? Shouldn't we have learned here at the ICTY from the Blaskic case that you should demand full disclosure before the trial so that the judgement you render is a reliable one and is the correct one? So those are the choices you make when we talk about specificity. I wish we could be more specific. This isn't a case about a murder that took place one night on the corner of Johan de Wittlaan and Scheveningsstraat. The charges in the indictment are extremely broad covering crimes over a six-month period involving 800.000 people, committed over the territory of Kosovo. General Ojdanic is not charged with being at the scene of any of these crimes but is charged with being a member of an amorphous joint criminal enterprise. The crime of this case must not only scrutinise his own conduct, what he said and what he did, but his role in this enterprise, his relationships and the foreseeability of the conduct of others. And the nature of these charges and the trial that will result from them make it impractical to be more specific, and that was recognised in the Kordic appeal decision. The Kordic appeal decision says the specificity clearly prohibits the use of broad categories as correctly asserted by the Prosecution prohibit the use of categories as such. A requested category of documents has to be defined with sufficient clarity to enable ready identification of documents falling within that category. Contrary to the assertion of the requesting state, this criterion does not automatically exclude all requests that involve the production of hundreds of documents. Considering the nature of the complex charges heard by the Tribunal, it is hard to see how that can be avoided. I submit to you that none of the states has made a factual showing that retrieval of the records sought will be unduly onerous, and in fact it appears that many of the states has not even tried -- have not even tried. The Government of Canada says that we have no basis to believe that Canada has any information responsive to the request. If that's the case, they need not be here. Every state which has searched its archives and told us that they don't have any responsive records, we've withdrawn our application for based on that representation. They've made no showing of any practical difficulties in retrieving the information or that they even tried. The representative from the Netherlands has told us that he's not sure if the information exists, but if he's ordered, he will look into the possibility of whether they have that information. The United Kingdom has not even tried to search and locate the intercepted conversations requested. I wonder how Professor Greenwood would react if he gave an assignment to one of his students and a student came back two years later and had done nothing and he said, "Your assignment wasn't specific enough. I have to trawl through an ocean to find what you asked for." I'd expect that the Professor Greenwood might ask, "Well, did you even try? Did you even do a simple word search to see what you came up with?" I don't think Professor Greenwood would accept those kind much excuses and neither should you. There's been no effort to comply and even try to retrieve these documents, and yet we have submitted a declaration from an expert who has shown from his knowledge and experience that retrieval of documents is not only possible but would not be onerous. The United States appears to have located from its vast archives records responsive to our request, as has the government of Germany indicated that they have and been able to search and find no material, although I don't fully understand whether or not that search was exhaustive enough and whether or not they're objecting on the grounds that the search is too burdensome if they've already completed the search. We made the request for intercepted conversations because we thought it would narrow the request, not broaden it. And I'm relating now to the question you asked, Judge Bonomy, of the United States, because if we just ask for all statements of General Ojdanic or all conversations, then we could get every time he's quoted in the news media or many, many other statements that would be in the possession not only of intelligence agencies but of agencies throughout all these governments, and so we specifically asked for intercepted conversations so that we could narrow our request only to the agencies that intercept and maintain such conversations. And now I think to come back and say that the request is too broad because it contains the word "intercepted conversations" I think defeats at least the purpose of what we were trying to accomplish. And with respect to the mechanics of an intercepted conversation which the state believes they have an interest not disclosing, we believe those are set forth fully in Rule 54 bis F and G which allow the state to take that intercepted conversation and submit it either in camera, ex parte, redacted are or in some cases not submitted at all but submit an affidavit from a responsible official. And so we believe we have been specific as possible under the circumstances and given the stakes involved. If you compare what we've asked for with the requests of the Prosecutor to Serbia and Montenegro that you have granted, you will see that our requests are no less specific.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Give us an example.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: The minutes of all --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You're going to read. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm going to give you the examples, yes. The minutes of all meetings of the supreme Defence council between 23 March 1999 and 5 October 2003 granted in your fifth decision on the 15th of September, 2003. The minutes of the assembly of the Republic of Serbia and the council for harmonisation of state policy between April 1990 and June 1997, a seven-year period, also in your fifth decision on applications on the 15th of September, 2003. Documentation relating to the joint command for Kosovo and Metohija for the period before and during the war. That's in your 13 this is decision on 17 December 2003, ruling 12A. And you granted request number 103, documentation in relation to investigations or prosecutions before any court, military or civilian, of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, Republic of Serbia, or the Republic of Montenegro for crimes committed in Kosovo between 1 January and 10 June 1999 by personnel including reservists of the army of Yugoslavia or of the Republic of Serbia Ministry of Internal Affairs. And that was in the 13th decision and the 2nd decision. There's no reasons why the intercepts of General Ojdanic between 1 January and 20 June should be treated any differently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Did you cite these in your written submissions?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, I didn't. All of these decisions came after our written submissions, actually.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: With respect to the issues of relevance and necessity, I think if you put yourself in the trial of General Ojdanic, the relevance and the necessity of the evidence sought becomes apparent. And I just want to focus for a minute on the third category of information sought, meetings between General Ojdanic and the representatives of countries. You've heard no reason why those records could not be produced. They're relevant to his knowledge and intent and you've heard so much similar evidence in the Milosevic case from these very countries. You've heard General Clark and Ambassador Walker from the United States testify as to statements made to them by President Milosevic and that's been admitted because it's relevant to President Milosevic's knowledge and his Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. intent. From the United Kingdom, Lord Ashdown testified to his conversations with President Milosevic. Relevant, necessary part of the case. Klaus Naumann likewise gave similar testimony and I submit to you there's no reason why any state who's had a representative -- had contact with General Ojdanic should not be providing that information. Now, what about the efforts to achieve voluntary compliance? I point out to you that ten countries were able to fulfil our requests, and I think it comes down to, that if the country wanted to fulfil the request, they could do it. If they wanted to raise obstacles, they could do that as well. Canada says that all voluntary means should be exhausted, but they never responded to our letters. They've raised all possible objections to disclosure of the information. They remain prepared to discuss all reasonable requests, but they cannot confirm nor deny that intercepted conversations exist. The Netherlands never answered our letter. The United Kingdom never answered our e-mail. They say they never received it until November 2002 when it was filed as an annex to our motion. But what did they do then? Did they ask for an extension to negotiate a resolution? No. They filed a pleading raising every possible objection. I suggest the ball was in their court, and instead of hitting it back to us, they stomped on it, they kicked it, and now they want you to declare them a winner because we didn't hit the ball back. It's good public lawyering to raise all these obstacles, but it's bad public policy for a trial chamber to accept them. The United States has spent a lot of time detailing the efforts that they made to provide us the information, but the -- always with the United States two things remained. First, they insisted that the information be provided pursuant to Rule 70, and it was impossible for us to accept that condition, because they insisted that the information would be provided on a confidential basis for the purpose of generating new evidence which is provided directly in the Rule, and that no testimony regarded this information that is provided by the US government could be offered or provided without the written consent of the United States government. Now, Prosecutors are in the business of generating leads for further investigation. That's not the purpose for which we need this material. We need this to use as evidence in the trial, and the United States always insisted as a condition of any production that we agree that before receiving anything, we cannot use it in evidence at this trial without their permission. And that is simply a condition that we can never accept. They also refused to provide intercepted conversations for us, saying that they with provide other statements of General Ojdanic that would not be intercepted conversations, which are the very conversations that we're looking for. So we tried. We met with then. We corresponded with them by e-mail, but it was clear to us that they were imposing conditions that we can never accept. So after the six month process of informal consultations, we concluded we were not going to get a single intercepted conversation from any of the countries at this hearing, and I think the events of this hearing and the last two years have shown that we were correct. I turn now to national security. We started off this hearing with the proposition that the disclosures of national security would be so sensitive that the hearing should be closed to members of the public. You've not had one concrete example of how the content of any intercepted conversation could possibly be damaging to national security, and it's the content that we want. We don't care what the methods were to obtain the conversation. We want the content, and that is -- there's been no showing of any national security interest that would be affected adversely by disclosing the content of General Ojdanic's conversation. But if they discover one, they are free to use the provisions of Rule 54 bis (F) and 54 bis (G) and submit that conversation to you in camera, ex parte, with all of the protections that Rule provides.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson, does that Rule not apply only prior to this hearing?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Lord Bonomy, I do not believe that's the case. I think that that Rule applies when a state has an objection to providing documents, whether that objection arises before being ordered to do so or after receiving an order under Rule 54 bis. I think, otherwise, we'd be dealing in the hypothetical with that, and we should be dealing with the actual reality of what do these intercepted conversations truly disclose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Or is it not because that -- because we are not dealing with specific items?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, we would never be dealing with a specific item in the sense that before the states produces the information there'd always be some degree of speculation as to the content of what is being asked to be produced. So it appears to me that the regime under Rule 54 bis (F) and (G) contemplates submission of the actual material to a Judge or a Trial Chamber, and we haven't reached the stage in this case. And I don't think even in a case of an order specific to one or two documents you would reach that stage until the document was actually produced or ordered to be produced to the Trial Chamber. In conclusion, I would --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt you, but I wonder if I can hear from you whether you are going to respond to the point raised by various states that what Defence is seeking is they're trying to prove a negative. Are you going to deal with that, or do you think it was dealt with by your earlier submission of today?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: I would like to deal with that, Judge Kwon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Because that is ancillary to the main purpose of receiving the interceptions, and that was addressed in our further submission as one further benefit in having a wide scope of intercepted conversations submitted to the Trial Chamber. One benefit of that would be that you could say that we now have the universe of intercepted conversations and nowhere in that universe of intercepted conversations either evidence that General Ojdanic participated in or had the intention to commit a war crime. That's an ancillary benefit to having the -- as many interceptions as possible produced before the Court, But it's not the main reason or motivation for seeking intercepted conversations. The motivation is for the content of the conversations themselves, that they will show, from the content of the conversations, that General Ojdanic -- what he did and what he said, and then you can infer from those -- the content whether or not he had the intention or participation in the crimes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is it not for the Prosecution to prove the accused is guilty, not for the accused to prove he's not guilty?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: It certainly is the burden initially on the Prosecutor to prove evidence sufficient for someone to be found guilty, but we can't sit back and simply say they haven't met their burden of proof. That's not how we intend to conduct a trial of someone who is factually innocent. We have an obligation to General Ojdanic and to this Trial Chamber to bring forth any evidence we could get our hands on that would show that General Ojdanic didn't commit these crimes. And although they have the burden of proof, that's -- it's not sufficient for us to sit back and say they haven't fulfilled it. It's necessary when defending someone, especially someone who is innocent, to bring forth evidence to prove, even though we don't have the obligation of it, but to prove that innocence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And I wonder whether Defence has received any of the materials which it is seeking from the state from the Prosecution so far, be it under Rule 66 or 68.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, not a thing. In fact, the intercepts that we obtained from Croatia pursuant to this procedure we disclosed to the Prosecution, and they have put that on their exhibit list as relevant evidence to be used during the trial. But we've not received, in all of the disclosure, any of the material that we're seeking by the Rule 54 bis order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson, you referred to the Milosevic order made in relation to Serbia, and you say that aspects of that order include requests which are as broad as this request and were, in fact, granted. I'm quite interested in that. It's one thing to cite the jurisprudence from the Appeals Chamber in Blaskic and Kordic, but I think it would have been useful if the submissions had centred more on recent decisions of Trial Chambers so that a comparison could be made. And, in fact, it strikes me that had you made those submissions in writing, then counsel for the respective states might have sought to distinguish those instances.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. I understand, and I'm happy to make such submissions in writing after this hearing if the Trial Chamber feels that those would be of any value.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, no. I only say that because we haven't had any submissions which have looked at orders made by this Trial Chamber, which I think is quite relevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, I agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just a minor point while you're on the subject. Was that application -- it was all the one application you were referring to; is that right? The order that you referred to made by this Chamber, it was just one order you referred to or was it more than one?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Actually, I was referring to three separate orders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: They weren't all on the same -- they were on three separate occasions, were they?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Was any of them opposed?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: I believe the government of Serbia and Montenegro opposed all of the orders. Just to be clear, I'm speaking of the 2nd, the 5th, and the 13th decision. And what I did was when I went through and looked -- compared the requests of the Prosecution in their pleadings with the item numbers listed in the Trial Chamber's orders to determine what was the scope of the request and which -- those which had been granted. In conclusion, members of the Trial Chamber and Mr. President, I'd like to emphasise that it is simply unacceptable for these states to create an International Tribunal to arrest an individual and imprison him in an international gaol, to hold a trial where witnesses from all these countries give evidence for the Prosecution, and at the same time to withhold from the Defence relevant evidence to the crimes to which he is charged. All of us have obligations here. As Trial Judges, you have an obligation to use your power to obtain all relevant evidence. As General Ojdanic's lawyer, I have an obligation to seek every piece of evidence that can help him during his trial. And under Article 29, the states have a clear obligation to cooperate with the production of documents with this International Tribunal. We all have a compelling responsibility to see that justice is done, and in this case if we fail, then a innocent man may well spend the rest of his life in prison. So I'd ask you to consider that when deliberating on this order, and if someone has to go the extra mile, I ask that you do so. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: There are three approaches reflected in the submissions by the states as to how this matter should be determined. Some states said the application should be dismissed and didn't make any comment on the possibility of a subsequent application being brought. One state, I believe Netherlands, said dismiss but appeared to envisage the possibility of a subsequent application. Another state, the united -- yes. Another state, the United Kingdom, said dismiss, dismiss outright, and without the possibility of a subsequent application being brought. May I bring -- may I bring your attention -- draw your attention to paragraph (H) of Rule 54 bis, which says: "Rejection of an application made under this Rule shall not preclude a subsequent application by the requesting party in respect of the same documents or information if new circumstances arise." And I wanted to ask Professor Greenwood, since he was quite emphatic about this, what comments he would have on this matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREENWOOD
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I don't wish there to be any misunderstanding about the nature of the British government's submissions. My submission yesterday was that the present application is misconceived, that it would not be possible from that application to craft an order, and therefore it is appropriate, in our submission, that the Tribunal dismiss the application outright. Now, I didn't speculate about the possibility of a fresh application being made. What I said in my submissions was that the correct way forward was for the Defence, if they wished to follow this matter up, to contact the governments and make a fateful application -- a faithful attempt to apply Rule 54 bis. Now, Of course, if at the end of that process they wish to make a fresh application to this Tribunal, then under Rule 54 bis (H), they would be able to do so. I hope that was what I said yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: If new circumstances arise. It depends on the interpretation of that phrase "new circumstances."

utterances.speaker: MR. GREENWOOD
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. If new circumstances arise. Now, whether those new circumstances would be contained in something in the correspondence between the Defence and the governments is another matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So can I take it as rule (H), Rule 54 bis (H), applies to the same document, so if specified later, is not -- cannot be considered as the same document which we are dealing with now. It's a bit different, but can I hear from you on that observation.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREENWOOD
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think that the answer would be that given the breadth of the present request, to make a fresh application requesting some of the documents that fell within the scope of that would be indeed an application for the same documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Professor Greenwood. I don't know whether Mr. Lammers of the Netherlands or any other representative would wish to comment on this issue. If not, I am to say that the Trial Chamber expresses its gratitude for all the submissions that have been made. We'll consider this matter and give a decision as soon as possible. The hearing is adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: at 5.52 p.m.
